review.material: All four printed pages (1–4), including the editors’ issue framing and discussion of its five contributions, were read.
review.limitations: This is a 2010 editorial, not a controlled experiment or a review of present-day building performance.

evidence.locator: pp. 2–4: five contributions and concluding synthesis
evidence.description: Editors’ summaries of other authors’ work; those studies were not independently replicated.

sections.title: What it is about
sections.text: Bier and Knight introduce an issue of Footprint devoted to architecture that uses digital systems to sense, respond and change. Their subject extends from digitally designing and fabricating a building to operating the built structure through feedback from its users and surroundings.

sections.title: The question
sections.text: What happens when architecture can change during use? The editorial asks how kinetic, responsive and interactive structures might address changing spatial needs, rather than treating the completed building as a permanently fixed configuration.

sections.title: Central premise
sections.text: The authors frame a shift from standardized, static production toward customizable and adaptable environments. They propose that digital control can support both practical flexibility and sensory or emotional relationships with buildings; these are possibilities to investigate, not measured benefits established by the editorial.

sections.title: How the argument works
sections.text: A short historical account connects contemporary systems with cybernetics, Archigram and kinetic architecture. The editors then compare five contributions spanning interactive design history, transformable structures, cultural interpretations, responsive installations and audiovisual extensions between spaces.

sections.title: Examples to watch
sections.text: The issue includes a scissor-pair transformable structure, an InteractiveWall combining sound, light and movement, and mediated windows connecting remote locations. These examples broaden interaction beyond mechanical movement to perception and communication. The descriptions belong to this editorial; detailed technical evidence is in the individual contributions.

sections.title: Conclusion and limits
sections.text: The editors argue that feedback-driven structures open new design possibilities, while identifying obstacles such as building regulations written around static forms. They provide no comparative energy, cost, safety or occupancy trial that establishes responsive architecture as generally superior.

sections.title: What to take into an experiment
sections.text: Distinguish designing an object digitally from designing its ongoing behaviour. For a responsive prototype, specify what it senses, what it changes, whose needs it serves and how feedback affects the next action. Use the cited projects to investigate those choices further.

terms.meaning: Built systems that change in relation to users or environmental conditions.
Information about a system or environment used to affect subsequent behaviour.
